overview.text: Auguste Rodin’s The Gates of Hell (La Porte de l’Enfer) is a monumental bronze portal conceived for a Paris museum that was never built. Commissioned in 1880, it began with Dante’s Inferno as inspiration, but Rodin’s imagery also came to explore human passions. More than 200 modeled figures crowd the doors; Rodin later reworked many as independent sculptures, including The Thinker and The Kiss. The project changed over time and remained unfinished when Rodin died. The Thinker was planned above the doors as Dante, but the figure later took on a broader meaning as a symbol of thought and creativity.

key_facts.text: The French state commissioned the portal in 1880 for a planned museum of decorative arts; that museum was never built.
Rodin based the project on Dante’s Divine Comedy, especially Inferno, and chose a design resembling a Gothic portal.
Rodin created more than 200 figures and groups for the doors, reusing figures such as The Thinker, The Kiss, and Ugolino in later works.
The Thinker was designed for the lintel above the doors, initially as Dante; Rodin later presented the figure more broadly as a thinker and creator.
The Gates were shown in a changed, fragmentary form in 1900. Rodin died before a bronze cast was made; a museum cast was produced in 1928.
